sections.overview: The red knot is a stocky Arctic-breeding wader that winters in huge, swirling flocks on estuaries. It is a long-distance migrant, and in Britain it depends on a small number of large estuaries.
sections.identification: In Britain an adult weighs about 138 g, with a wing near 169 mm, roughly Blackbird-sized and larger than a Dunlin. The bill is straight and about as long as the head, and the legs have a greenish tint. In winter it is pale grey above and white below; in spring and summer the face, chest and belly turn brick-red. Young birds look scalloped.
sections.habitat: In winter and on migration it feeds on muddy and sandy shores, especially large estuaries, and it is generally absent from rocky coasts. It breeds on high, barren Arctic tundra, usually near a pond or stream.
sections.diet: Away from the breeding grounds the red knot eats small invertebrates from intertidal mud, mainly small molluscs, with some marine worms and crustaceans. On the Arctic tundra it feeds mostly on insects, especially flies, and early in the season on plant material.
sections.behavior: Outside the breeding season knots gather in large flocks that flash their pale underwings as they twist and turn. They breed in the Arctic and migrate south in autumn, with a pronounced passage through the UK. Some birds from the Canadian Arctic apparently cross the Greenland ice cap to winter in Britain and Europe.
sections.reproduction: A pair typically raises one brood a year, laying four eggs (sometimes three) in a shallow ground scrape lined with leaves, lichen and moss. Both sexes incubate for 21–22 days, and the chicks fledge after about 18–20 days. Breeding usually starts at two years of age.
sections.ecology: Knots rely on a few rich estuaries as feeding grounds both on migration and in winter, so changes there matter greatly. Threats named include barrages, sea-level rise and human disturbance of feeding areas; in North America, the loss of horseshoe crab eggs at Delaware Bay has hit the species hard.
sections.conservation: The IUCN Red List classes the species as Near Threatened, and it is Amber-listed in the UK. About 265,000 knots winter in the UK (2012–17); BTO reports a 15% rise between 1998 and 2023, while the RSPB describes an earlier 13% fall over 25 years. The oldest ringed bird lived over 27 years.
